European Parliament Plenary Debate
Date: 2026-04-29
Topic: Стратегия на ЕС в отговор на продължаващата криза в Близкия 

President: – The first item is the debate on Council and Commission statements on the 'EU strategy in response to the ongoing Middle East crisis, its implications on energy prices and the availability of fertilizers' (

Marilena | Raouna: It is abundantly clear that the ongoing crisis in the Middle East carries profound global repercussions that directly impact the Union's security, environment and interests. As noted in this hemicycle last month, this conflict is neither abstract nor distant. Quite the contrary – it is in our neighbourhood. It has wide ranging consequences on our security and economies, and it requires us as the European Union to actively engage and act

in unity with a coherent and coordinated approach. Acting in unity also requires clarity of messaging and action, including on what to achieve in the long run. This includes restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in line with international law and UNCLOS, with no caveats or restrictions, working and contributing towards de-escalation that can pave the way for a lasting ceasefire and long-term peace and stability, and working to ensure that Iran does not acquire or develop the capacity to produce nuclear weapons. To achieve these objectives, our cooperation with our Middle East and Gulf partners is not merely important – it is a necessity. The Union has maintained regular and close contact at different levels with countries in the region. We have expressed solidarity with

our regional partners who have been attacked and affected by this war. Partners who have shown to be reliable even in the midst of attacks on their territory. We have reiterated our commitment to work with them for stability, while at the same time working to expand our dialogue and our strategic cooperation. In this regard, we have welcomed the ceasefire agreed by the United States and Iran on 9 April. We encourage parties to continue engaging in good faith. Diplomacy remains the only viable path towards restoring stability. The EU will continue to contribute to all diplomatic efforts in line with its consistent, reliable role, drawing on its diplomatic reach, experience and long-term partnerships. These core messages were clearly articulated both by the European Union and regional leader

s last Friday in Nicosia, in a productive meeting in the margins of the informal leaders meeting between the European Union and leaders from Lebanon, Egypt, Syria, Jordan and the Gulf. Honourable Members, as mentioned, safeguarding freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz is a primary concern given the massive impact on EU competitiveness, the energy market and the impact on prices and cost of living. Disruption to energy and global trade flows and prices trigger ripple effects on fertiliser supply, on food prices, on economic growth, as well as on investment partners. In the context of safeguarding freedom of navigation, the role of EU maritime defensive operation ASPIDES that is providing a critical contribution to keeping one of the world's most vital waterways open and secure, is

critical. In parallel, the Council is fully committed to working on new proposals that would help mitigate the impact of the crisis on energy prices, directly reflecting the conclusions agreed during the European Council in March, the 'One Europe, One Market' roadmap, which was co-signed in Cyprus in the margins of the informal leaders' summit by the three institutions. There is no silver bullet – as long as the EU continues to depend on imported fossil fuels, we will remain vulnerable to price spikes. It is clear that European strategic autonomy, European independence goes hand-in-hand with energy security. That is why it is essential to stay the course on our energy transition goals in expanding domestically generated and affordable energy, together with short-term measures agreed to mit

igate energy spikes. Our strategy is twofold: on the one hand, implementing immediate measures to stabilise energy prices while simultaneously forging a robust energy union to secure our long-term strategic independence. The grids package is an essential part of this effort. Regarding fertilisers, we are looking forward to receiving the Commission's action plan, in the context of which we look to short-term measures to respond to the current circumstances, as well as measures to increase the resilience of the EU agricultural sector by reducing our reliance on imports. While we tackle the effects of the conflict in Iran, we cannot lose sight of the other sources of tension in the Middle East. Lebanon is paying a heavy price for a war it did not choose. Too many have lost their lives, and we

have seen attacks on UN peacekeepers, which is unacceptable. We welcome the ceasefire and ongoing preparatory talks under US auspices, and we urge all sides to end hostilities and fully respect Lebanon's sovereignty and territorial integrity. We also cannot lose sight of the situation in Gaza and the West Bank. There needs to be progress on the implementation of the Gaza peace plan, in the absence of which there is a risk of undermining the fragile political momentum. With all that this entails, including providing Hamas with the opportunity to consolidate control. The EU remains committed to do its part with all the tools at its disposal. In this framework, we convened last week two important international meetings in Brussels: that of the Global Alliance and that of the Ad Hoc Liaison C

ommittee. Ultimately, just and sustainable peace can only be reached on the basis of a two-state solution in line with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions.

Ursula | von der Leyen: So our message is very clear: we will continue our support to the brave Ukrainian people and their armed forces. While Russia is doubling down on its aggression, Europe doubles down on our support for Ukraine. That day we also adopted the 20th sanctions package. And yes, the sanctions are biting. They have a biting effect on the Russian economy. With inflation increasing and interest rates skyrocketing, the consequences of Russia's war of choice are also being paid for out of Russian people's pockets.
